This document exists for non-obvious, error-prone shortcomings in the codebase, the model, or the tooling that an agent cannot figure out by reading the code alone. No architecture overviews, file trees, build commands, or standard behavior. When you encounter something that belongs here, first consider whether a code change could eliminate it and suggest that to the user. Only document it here if it can't be reasonably fixed.

---

## pitfalls

- templates are dual-source: official/community via graphql, user via rest; list/search merge results and apply search/pagination client-side; graphql failures are intentionally best-effort.
- graphql template shapes are inconsistent: `ports` may be string or array, `env` is key/value pairs; normalize before output and only return `readme/env/ports` on `template get`.
- `doctor` is the only mutating setup path (api key + ssh sync); onboarding/ssh changes must update both `cmd/doctor` and `internal/sshconnect` hints.
- legacy commands must preserve stdout and behavior exactly; deprecation warnings go to stderr only (exec is the most common regression).
- CON-683 exception to the above: errors must never reach stdout. `api/query.go` and `internal/api/graphql.go` return the typed `no_credentials` sentinel instead of printing; `cmd/model` and `cmd/exec` return every error to the `Execute` sink. still unconverted, and still violating this: `cmd/pod/*Pod.go`, `cmd/pods/*`, `cmd/cloud` (plaintext via `cobra.CheckErr`) and `cmd/project/*` (prints to stdout and exits 0 — CON-874 deletes the command rather than fixing it). see `TestLegacyCommandKeepsStdoutCleanWithoutAPIKey`.
- `cmd/project.go` is not wired into the cli; the hidden `project` command is created in `cmd/root.go` and wraps `cmd/project/*`.
- any test that `Execute()`s a *runnable* command must redirect `HOME` (and `USERPROFILE`) to `t.TempDir()`. `cobra.OnInitialize(initConfig)` fires from the hook chain, ahead of every `PersistentPreRunE`, and `initConfig` writes `~/.runpod/config.toml` whenever it can't read one — so such a test creates a real config, and on an unreadable one overwrites it with defaults and destroys the developer's stored api key. `--help`-only tests don't hit this: cobra returns before the initializers. cannot be fixed in the test alone — `OnInitialize` is a cobra package global that runs for any root you build.
- `initConfig` runs from `cobra.OnInitialize`, i.e. ahead of every `PersistentPreRunE`, and `cmd/config/config.go:114` binds `--apiKey` into viper at package init. so a *rejected* `config --apiKey=… --output=table` still persists that key to a freshly created `~/.runpod/config.toml`. no validation in the hook chain can prevent this; only moving `initConfig` after the hooks would.
- `--output` is validated in the root `PersistentPreRunE`, which means it only guards commands cobra actually runs. `--help`, `help <cmd>`, a bare parent, `--version`/`-v` and completion all resolve earlier and skip it; `help` additionally needs the explicit exemption in that hook so a bad `--output` can't hide the help that lists valid values.
- api accepts `gpuTypeIds` arrays, but the cli is intentionally singular (`--gpu-id`); multi-id fallback must be an explicit new flag.
- pod creation uses graphql (`podFindAndDeployOnDemand`) because the rest api rejects `startSsh` — do not move pod create to rest without confirming `startSsh` support.
- graphql `dataCenterId` is singular; rest uses `dataCenterIds` (plural). graphql `ports` is a comma-separated string; rest uses `[]string`. graphql `env` returns `["KEY=VALUE"]`; rest uses `map[string]string`. graphql takes a raw `dockerArgs` string; rest has no `dockerArgs` field (rejects it as an extra key) — shlex-split into `dockerStartCmd` instead (see `splitDockerArgs`).
- serverless create is graphql-only (`saveEndpoint`); the rest `/endpoints` create path is intentionally unused so model references + multi-region volumes + all flags work on one path. do not reintroduce rest routing.
- `saveEndpoint.gpuIds` wants gpu *pool* ids (e.g. `ADA_24`), not the gpu *type* ids (e.g. `NVIDIA A40`) that `gpu list` / `--gpu-id` use; translate via `serverlessGpuPools` (`ResolveServerlessGpuPoolID`). pod create uses type ids directly — different identifier space.
- rest `/pods` and `/pods/{id}` never return `runtime` — `api.Pod.Runtime` is never populated by prod. runtime telemetry only exists on graphql `Pod.runtime`, and `runtime == null` is the only "container not up yet" signal there is (the resolver returns null on any hapi error, 404 included). derive states via `internal/podstate`, never ad hoc.
- graphql `Pod.uptimeSeconds` is deprecated *and always 0* in prod, and its deprecation notice points at a `runtime.uptimeSeconds` that does not exist; the real field is `runtime.uptimeInSeconds`.
- a stopped (EXITED) pod keeps reporting stale non-null `runtime` with a climbing `uptimeInSeconds` for a while, so runtime presence must only be consulted after `desiredStatus == RUNNING`.
- `PodStopReason` (IMAGE_PULL_ERROR etc.) is a podStop *input* only: not persisted, not queryable. `lastStatusChange` is free text and is the only attribution available; the backend spells the platform both "Runpod" and "RunPod", so match it case-insensitively. the full set it writes is `Rented by User:`, `Bid by user:`, `Exited by {user,Runpod}:`, `Terminated by {user,RunPod}:` and `Outbid:` — the last is the only recorded *cause*, everything else is just an actor.
- a terminate writes `desiredStatus: EXITED`, **not** TERMINATED, with `lastStatusChange` = `Terminated by {user,RunPod}:` (`model/src/pod/terminatePod.ts:218`/`:276`, `terminateAllStoppedPods.ts:80`, `cluster/deleteCluster.ts:129`/`:210`). the only writers of TERMINATED are the two outbid paths (`model/src/utils/index.ts:495`, `resumePod.ts:570`). both also set `terminatedAt`, which `getMyPods` filters on (`:107`/`:128`), so a terminated pod drops out of the list surfaces rather than being reported.
- `pod update --ports` is a wholesale replacement, not additive (`req.Ports = strings.Split(...)` in `cmd/pod/update.go`; `ports: input.ports` in `model/src/pod/editJob.ts:161`) — unlike `--env`, which merges. it also bumps `version`, and the host names containers `{podId}-{version}` (`host/pkg/dockpose/api.go:215`), so a port change can recreate the container. never suggest `--ports X` without the pod's existing ports in it.
- the image-pull state is not dropped on the host, only on the graphql path: podsync pushes "still fetching image" into hapi's log store, served publicly at `/v2/pods/{id}/logs` on `v2-rest.runpod.io` (a different base url than this cli's `rest.runpod.io/v1`, but it accepts the same key). it is free text for humans, not a state to branch on.
- graphql `Pod.desiredStatus` and rest `/pods/{id}.desiredStatus` are separate snapshots and can disagree; anything derived from `runtime` must be gated on the desiredStatus from the *same* snapshot, or momentary skew silently defeats the gate (both `cmd/pod/get.go` and `cmd/pod/list.go` derive via `sshconnect.PodState(gqlPod)` while still publishing rest's `desiredStatus`).
- prod graphql has introspection disabled; probe field names by querying them and reading the "Cannot query field X on type Y" validation error.
- invoking an endpoint (`serverless health/run/status`, and `serverless create --wait`'s readiness poll) hits a *different service* from the control plane: `api.runpod.ai/v2`, via `api.InvokeClient` (`internal/api/invoke.go`), not `api.Client`/`c.request`. both resolve the host through `invokeBaseURL()`, so `RUNPOD_INVOKE_URL` moves the reported urls and the calls together — never hardcode the host again. `InvokeClient` is the only transport to that service: `EndpointHealth` returns the raw body (for printing) and `EndpointHealthCounts` decodes it (for branching), so do not add a second client for it. it has no client-wide timeout on purpose — every call must carry a context deadline, which is why the `--wait` poll wraps its read in one.
- `/runsync` is unused by the cli on purpose (`serverless run` submits on `/run` and polls `/status`), even though `serverless get` still reports its url. it is not "sync": the invoke api holds the connection for 90s (`waitInt := 90000` in ai-api `pkg/api/runsync.go`) and then answers with a still-running job, so `/status` polling is required either way. worse, no job id exists until it responds, so a slow response strands a billed, unpollable job; and a `sync-`-prefixed job's result is expired after 1 minute vs 30 minutes for `/run` (ai-api `pkg/job/job.go`, `strings.HasPrefix(requestId, "sync-")`). do not "optimise" run back onto `/runsync`.
- the invoke api decodes the request body into a struct whose `input` is a json *object* (ai-api `job.JobInput`), so an array or scalar payload is a 400. `serverless run` rejects it locally as `usage_error` instead.
- `serverless run/status` add two error codes to the vocabulary in `internal/api/client.go`: `timeout` and `job_failed` (terminal status other than `COMPLETED`). a `job_failed`/`timeout` run still prints the job payload on stdout and exits 1 — the worker's own error is the useful artifact, and it is data, not an error object.
- `timeout` covers two different outcomes and the message is the only thing that separates them: a `--wait` budget that ran out with the job still running server-side (message names the `serverless status` follow-up; do not re-invoke), and a single invoke call that exceeded the per-call `timeout` config key (`health`, a plain `status`, the submit — nothing is left running, a retry is correct). `internal/api/invoke.go`'s `do()` turns *any* context deadline into a `TimeoutError`, so do not narrow the documented meaning to "the work is still running" — the control plane reports the same condition as `network_error`, which is the closest analogue. `model add --wait-for-hash` was `cli_error` before this and is now `timeout`.
- a job payload and the health body are third-party data, so they go out through `output.PrintRaw`, not `output.Print`. `Print` rewrites `gpuTypeId`->`gpuId` (right for the cli's own control-plane structs, wrong for a handler's keys) and round-trips through `map[string]interface{}`, which turns every number into a float64 and corrupts integers above 2^53.
- a 200 from the invoke api is not necessarily a job: a body with neither `id` nor `status` is a bare error object. `api.Job.HasEnvelope` guards it, otherwise `run` would exit 0 on a failed request and print a follow-up `serverless status` command with an empty job id. `HasEnvelope` is satisfied by a bare `status`, so it does *not* cover a submit that returns a status and no id — `invokeJob`'s `--no-wait` branch has its own `NewNoJobIDError` guard for that, and `waitForTerminal` captures the job id once up front rather than re-reading it from each poll response.
- `saveEndpoint` has no `computeType`: cpu is selected by sending `instanceIds` like `cpu3g-4-16` (gpu is the default when instanceIds is empty). `name` is required (`String!`, min 3) and is never auto-generated server-side — generate one client-side. flashboot is the `flashBootType` enum (`OFF`/`FLASHBOOT`), not a bool. multi-region volumes are `networkVolumeIds: [{networkVolumeId}]`, not a flat string array.
- `--wait` readiness signals are not the obvious fields: a pod's port 22 shows up in `runtime.ports` (graphql; rest leaves `runtime` null) minutes before sshd listens, and prod allocates it even for images with no sshd — so readiness is a tcp connect plus an ssh banner, never the port listing. an endpoint's `includeWorkers` list is historical: every worker on a warm, healthy endpoint reads `desiredStatus: EXITED` while `/health` reports them ready, so worker readiness comes from `/health` (invoke service, `RUNPOD_INVOKE_URL`). neither `/health` counter means "hot handler" and there is no third one: `ready` counts flashboot-cached workers (`ai-api/pkg/api/health.go` `counts()` buckets an `EXITED` pod as ready when `workerstate.IsReady`), and `running` counts `desiredStatus: RUNNING`, which is written when the worker row is created — i.e. at scheduling time, before any container exists (`runpod-backend/model/src/pod/rentPod.ts`). `running` still has to count, because a `workersMin` worker stays `RUNNING` forever and never enters `ready`. `workersMin 0` does **not** mean "no worker ever starts": `finalEndpoint` floors `workersStandby` to 5 whenever `workersMax > 1` (`ai-api/pkg/graphql/aiapi.go`), `worker.Sync` fills it with cache workers (`pkg/worker/sync.go`), and every `/health` read triggers a `Sync` (`pkg/loader/aiapi.go`) — so `--wait` at 0 min workers warns, it is not refused.
- a wait must treat poll errors as "state unknown" and keep going, because the resource already exists and bills; reporting a transport code would tell an agent to retry the create and buy a second one. only these end it early: http `400`/`401`/`403` or the codes `unauthorized`/`forbidden`/`no_credentials`/`bad_request`, a terminal pod status (`conflict`), and a resource missing from **two consecutive** reads (`not_found`) — or, for a resource that has never been readable at all, from twelve consecutive reads (`missesBeforeKnown`, ~1 min at the default interval, and only if `--wait-timeout` is longer than that), so an endpoint deleted or mistyped before `/health` ever answered, or a pod terminated before it was ever listed, does not burn the whole budget and then report `wait_timeout`. both waits enforce it. the status check is load-bearing, not redundant: the pod wait's only api call is graphql, and every graphql failure is an `*api.GraphQLError` whose `ErrorCode()` is the constant `graphql_error`, so a bad key would otherwise burn the whole budget and report `wait_timeout`. `404`/`429`/`5xx` stay transient — `/health` 404s an endpoint id it has not propagated yet. errors that leave a billed resource behind carry its id in the error object's `id` field (`internal/output.WithResourceID`), not only in the message.

## constraints

- all text output must be lowercase and concise.
- default output format is json (for agent consumption); never change this default.
- e2e tests cost real money — always clean up resources with `t.Cleanup`.
- always e2e test cli changes before considering work done: build the binary, run the new/changed commands against the live api (`RUNPOD_API_KEY` is in the env), and clean up any created resources immediately after verifying the response. this is non-negotiable.
- keep the runpodctl skill in sync: https://github.com/runpod/runpod-plugins-official/tree/main/plugins/runpod/skills/runpodctl — update it whenever commands, flags, or behavior change.
